strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: measuring social biases in masked language models and tracking changes after continued training.

The experiments cover four model checkpoints, two established benchmarks, multiple bias categories, and relevant likelihood-based baselines. Detailed category-level results help expose differences across models and datasets.

Training separately on stereotypical and anti-stereotypical sentences provides a useful sensitivity experiment. The proposed scores generally respond in the expected direction, supporting a narrower contribution about detecting changes in sentence preference.
weaknesses: The central claim of more accurate social-bias measurement is insufficiently validated. Prediction quality can reflect lexical frequency, linguistic plausibility, and memorization as well as stereotypical associations. Disagreement with existing metrics does not establish that those metrics underestimate religious or disability bias, as repeatedly claimed. Independent validation or appropriate control conditions are needed.

The retraining experiment does not separate generalizable bias changes from fitting the evaluation sentences. Section 4.3 describes an 80/20 training/validation split of CrowS-Pairs, but reports bias scores on the same benchmark without an independent held-out bias evaluation. The reported 100% accuracy measures agreement with assumed training-direction labels across 72 aggregate conditions; it does not establish accurate measurement of social bias.

Human-annotation evidence is weak. Figure 3 reports best AUCs of 0.571 versus 0.569 for the strongest baseline on BERT, and 0.572 versus 0.566 on RoBERTa. These small gains, with only 58 negative pairs and no confidence intervals or comparison tests, do not establish superiority. Moreover, annotations concern whether sentence pairs express stereotypes, rather than whether a particular model exhibits bias. The pair-level scoring and threshold-selection procedure also needs clarification.

Several statistical interpretations are unsupported. Section 4.2 infers differences between models from significant versus nonsignificant within-model tests, without directly testing the model difference; Welch's test also disregards the paired sentence design. The McNemar tests concern changes in binary preference labels, whereas Equation 16 measures increases in continuous preference differences. These are different quantities, so the significance markers do not directly validate the reported change scores.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite public datasets and named checkpoints. The manuscript provides no implementation link and omits learning rates, optimizer settings, batch sizes, random seeds, split details, and precise attention aggregation. Equations 1–2 sum over all sentence tokens despite describing different target-token subsets, leaving baseline implementation fidelity uncertain.

The proposed change score needs additional specification: Equation 16 assigns unchanged pairs to the same outcome as decreases, so identical models receive a score of zero rather than a neutral result. Tie handling is particularly relevant to rank-based measures. Together with the validation and reproducibility gaps, this prevents a sound Findings recommendation at present; targeted methodological corrections and additional experiments warrant resubmission next cycle.
